content:
A hands-on look at what happens after you fine-tune: where the memory goes, where it breaks, and why small is cheap.

7 min read
Just now

--

Last time, I fine-tuned a small AI model on my Mac to do one narrow job — read an app-store review and turn it into tidy structured data — and showed it costs about nothing to do yourself. That article was about making the model.
New here? In Part 1 I took a small, off-the-shelf AI model and fine-tuned it — trained it on a few hundred examples to do one narrow job: read an app-store review and turn it into tidy structured data (positive or negative, what it’s about, the star rating it implies). It ran on a Mac mini on my desk and cost less than a cent. This part picks up right after: I have the model — now what does it cost to run? Link at the bottom, you don’t need it now.
This one is about a different, less glamorous question that turns out to matter far more in the real world: once you have a model, what does it actually cost to run it?
Training a model is a one-time event. Running it happens millions of times — every review, every request, forever. That’s where the real cost lives: memory, speed, electricity.
I went looking for exactly where my little model spends those things, inspired by a whitepaper on squeezing giant models onto phones.
